title: Tuples & Sets
overview: Python gives you the right tool for the job. Lists are great, but sometimes you need data that shouldn't change, or data where duplicates don't matter. Tuples and sets solve exactly these problems.

blocks.content: Some data should never change. The days of the week. The cardinal directions. Your date of birth. Using a list for this — which can be accidentally modified — is risky.
A **tuple** is like a list, but **immutable** — once created, it cannot be changed. You define it with parentheses `()` instead of square brackets.

blocks.title: Try It — Creating Tuples
blocks.code:
# Tuple of days
days = ("Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun")

# Access like a list
print(days[0])   # Mon
print(days[-1])  # Sun
print(len(days)) # 7

# Iterate like a list
for day in days:
    print(day)
blocks.expectedOutput:
Mon
Sun
7
Mon
Tue
Wed
Thu
Fri
Sat
Sun

blocks.content: Tuples support indexing, slicing, and loops — just like lists. The difference: you cannot append, remove, or change any item.

blocks.title: Try It — Tuple Unpacking
blocks.code:
# GPS coordinates — should never change
location = (13.0827, 80.2707)  # Chennai

# Unpack into separate variables
latitude, longitude = location

print(f"Latitude: {latitude}")
print(f"Longitude: {longitude}")

analogy.title: Passport Information
analogy.description: Your passport has fixed details — name, date of birth, nationality. These values should never accidentally change. A tuple is like a digital passport: the data is locked in. You can read it, but not modify it.
bullets: Your passport contains fixed, official data — name, DOB, nationality.
Once issued, you cannot change passport details yourself.
The data must stay unchanged to remain valid and trustworthy.
analogy.highlightCard: A tuple stores data that should never change — it's immutable by design.

visualization.title: List vs Tuple
visualization.condition: Does the data need to change?
bullets: Tuples use round brackets (), lists use square brackets [].
Once created, a tuple cannot be modified — no append, no remove.
Use tuples for data that must stay constant: coordinates, dates, config.
visualization.highlightCard: tuple = immutable. list = mutable. Choose based on whether the data should change.

highlights: passport[0] accesses 'Rohan' — reading works just like a list.
Trying to modify passport[0] raises a TypeError — tuples cannot change.
code.highlightCard: Use a tuple when the data must remain constant. Use a list when it can change.

reflection.question: When should you use a tuple instead of a list?
reflection.answer: When the data is fixed and shouldn't change — like coordinates, days of the week, or constant configuration values.
options: When data is fixed and shouldn't change
When you need more than 10 items
When items are all the same type

blocks.content: What if you need to store a collection of unique values where order doesn't matter? That's a set.
A **set** automatically removes duplicates. If you add the same value twice, the set keeps only one copy. Sets use curly braces `{}`.

blocks.title: Try It — Sets Remove Duplicates
blocks.code:
# Votes cast — may have duplicates
votes = {"Alice", "Bob", "Alice", "Charlie", "Bob", "Alice"}

print(votes)          # Duplicates removed
print(len(votes))     # Only 3 unique voters

blocks.content: Sets are **unordered** — the items have no guaranteed position. You can't use index `[0]` on a set. But you can iterate, check membership, and perform set operations.

blocks.title: Try It — Set Operations
blocks.code:
python_students = {"Ravi", "Meera", "Arjun", "Priya"}
java_students = {"Meera", "Kiran", "Priya", "Sana"}

# Union: all students
print("All:", python_students | java_students)

# Intersection: both courses
print("Both:", python_students & java_students)

# Difference: only Python
print("Only Python:", python_students - java_students)

analogy.title: School Club Members
analogy.description: Two school clubs post their member lists. Some students are in both. The union is everyone in either club. The intersection is students in both clubs. The difference is students in only one club. Set operations answer these real-world questions instantly.
bullets: A club has a unique member list — no one can join twice.
Adding an existing member has no effect on the roster.
Membership checks are instant — the list is always clean.
analogy.highlightCard: A set stores only unique values — duplicates are automatically removed.

visualization.title: Set Operations
bullets: Sets use curly braces {} and automatically remove any duplicates.
You can find which members two sets share (intersection) or who is in either (union).
Set operations like union, intersection, and difference work instantly.
visualization.highlightCard: set = unique values only. union = all of both. intersection = common to both.

highlights: set() or {} creates a set — duplicates are silently dropped.
drama | art gives the union (everyone in either club).
drama & art gives the intersection (members in both clubs).
code.highlightCard: Sets handle membership, uniqueness, and group comparisons better than lists.

sections.label: List vs Tuple vs Set — When to Use Which

blocks.content: Having three sequence types can feel confusing at first. But each has a clear purpose.

**Use a List when:** order matters, items may change, duplicates are allowed.

**Use a Tuple when:** data is fixed and should not be modified, often used for coordinates, RGB values, or function return values.

**Use a Set when:** you need only unique values, order doesn't matter, or you need set math (union, intersection).

blocks.title: Try It — Choosing the Right Type
blocks.code:
# List: student marks that will be updated
marks = [78, 85, 90, 67]
marks.append(92)

# Tuple: fixed course structure
course = ("Python 2.0", 14, "Beginner")

# Set: unique enrolled students
enrolled = {"Ravi", "Priya", "Meera"}
enrolled.add("Arjun")

print(marks)
print(course)
print(enrolled)

analogy.title: Notebook, Stone Tablet, Unique Numbers Box
analogy.description: A notebook (list) — you write in it, erase, add pages. A stone tablet (tuple) — carved once, read forever, never changed. A box of unique lottery numbers (set) — only one of each number, order doesn't matter, automatically rejects duplicates.
bullets: A notebook is flexible — you can add, erase, and reorder content.
A stone tablet is permanent — once carved, the data cannot change.
A unique collection discards anything you try to add twice.
analogy.highlightCard: list, tuple, and set each solve a different problem — know which to use when.

visualization.title: Choosing the Right Tool
bullets: list: ordered, changeable, allows duplicates — your go-to for most collections.
tuple: ordered, unchangeable, allows duplicates — for permanent, fixed data.
set: unordered, changeable, no duplicates — for unique items and group operations.
visualization.highlightCard: list = flexible. tuple = permanent. set = unique. Match the structure to the need.

code.code:
# Quick type test
print(type([1, 2, 3]))    # list
print(type((1, 2, 3)))    # tuple
print(type({1, 2, 3}))    # set
highlights: Use list when order matters and items will be added or removed.
Use tuple when the data must stay fixed — like coordinates or dates.
Use set when you only care about what's present, not how many times.
code.highlightCard: Choosing the right structure makes your code cleaner, faster, and more intentional.

reflection.question: You're storing the 7 days of the week — which type is best?
reflection.answer: Tuple — days of the week are fixed (never change) and ordered (Mon through Sun). A tuple communicates that intention clearly.
options: Set — because the names are unique

keyTakeaways.text: Tuples use () and are immutable — created once, never changed.
Tuples support indexing, slicing, and iteration — just like lists.
Tuple unpacking: a, b = (1, 2) assigns items to individual variables.
Sets use {} and automatically remove duplicates.
Sets are unordered — no indexing allowed.
Rule of thumb: List = changeable, Tuple = fixed, Set = unique.

quiz.question: Which of the following is a tuple?
quiz.explanation: Tuples use parentheses (). Square brackets [] are lists, curly braces {} without colons are sets, and {} with colons are dictionaries.

quiz.question: What happens when you add a duplicate to a set?
options: It is silently ignored — sets only store unique values
quiz.answer: It is silently ignored — sets only store unique values
quiz.explanation: Sets automatically maintain uniqueness. Adding a value that already exists does nothing — no error, no duplicate. This is actually a feature, not a bug.

quiz.question: What does the & operator do with sets?
options: Intersection — items present in BOTH sets
Difference — items in the first but not second
quiz.answer: Intersection — items present in BOTH sets
quiz.explanation: The & operator returns the intersection — only items that appear in both sets. Use | for union (all items from both) and - for difference.

quiz.question: Can you modify a tuple after creation?
quiz.explanation: Immutability is the defining feature of tuples. Once created, you cannot add, remove, or change any element. This makes tuples safe to use as dictionary keys and guarantees the data won't be accidentally changed.

quiz.question: What does set([1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3]) produce?
quiz.explanation: set() converts a list to a set, automatically removing duplicates. The result {1, 2, 3} has only the unique values.

problems.title: Common Friends

problems.description:

Convert to a set to remove duplicates, then convert back to a sorted list and print it.

Expected output:
[1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 9]
